schools.summary: Gregory the Great: the friends, trained by habit to good living but not to an exact estimate of God's judgments, could not conceive that a righteous man might suffer ills, and so judged Job wicked because they saw him scourged.
Gill: regardless of Job's distress, plea, and confession, Zophar starts up and attacks with as much heat and passion as ever, still representing Job as a wicked man and a hypocrite.
Henry: Zophar, resolved to condemn Job for a bad man, is displeased that he talks so like a good one; the doctrine will be well explained and worst applied.
Clarke lays out the plan of the whole speech — the wretchedness of the wicked and hypocrite, their short rejoicing, ruin in family and person, stripped wealth, and violent death.
Ellicott: Zophar retorts with yet greater vehemence and a more ornate, elaborate style, reiterating the old burden of the speedy doom of the wicked.

themes: the movement of the second speech

schools.summary: Gill takes Zophar at his own valuation: his thoughts, coming thick and fast, constrain him to answer, and he is anxious it be understood his reply proceeded from thought and mature deliberation.

Clarke calls Zophar the most inveterate of Job's adversaries, rendering the verse (with Good) 'whither would my tumult transport me?' — the Hebrew, 'there is sensibility in me'; Wesley: he makes haste, speaking sooner than intended, perhaps interrupting Job.

Ellicott: the 'therefore' points back to the eagerness stirring him to reply; Keil and Delitzsch reject Schultens's 'perturbatio animi' for the crux and read the clause as an apology for the vehemence to follow.

themes: the crux of the second clause

schools.summary: Gill gives two constructions: Zophar heard Job's reproof (the warning of the sword) and could not bear it; or he pretends to a divine oracle, a confutation heard from God with which he is furnished to answer.
Clarke: Zophar quotes Job's 'ten times ye reproached me' (ch. 19:3) and retracts nothing, sure his judgment cannot err; Wesley: 'I speak not from passion, but from certain knowledge.'
Ellicott: 'the reproof of my shame'; 'out of my understanding my spirit answereth me' — Zophar moved by an inward impulse he cannot but obey.

debates.question: What is 'the spirit of my understanding' from which Zophar answers?

sides.position: an offended, impatient spirit stung by Job's reproof
a pretended divine oracle, or certain knowledge and not passion

themes: a divine oracle or mere pique

schools.summary: Gill renders 'of old' as 'from eternity' — an ancient and established maxim, not Zophar's novelty, which the knowing man Job must surely own.
Clarke fixes 'since Adam was placed on the earth': a maxim as old as the world, with a thrust at Job's late confidence about a general judgment.
Henry: an appeal to Job's own conviction and the experience of all ages — since man was made, the sin of sinners has been his ruin (Acts 28:4; Isa. 3:11).
Keil and Delitzsch render the solemn preface, 'knowest thou this which is from everlasting, since man was placed upon the earth.'

themes: a maxim as old as the race
since man was on the earth

schools.summary: Gill: the friends, once denying the wicked prosper at all, now grant it but for a little while; the Hebrew sets the triumph 'from near,' begun lately and quickly ended.

Ellicott: the destruction of the wicked is not only certain but speedy (cf. Ps. 103:16; Job 7:8); Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet as one measured verdict on a prosperity allowed only to be pronounced brief.
Henry seizes on 'hypocrite,' Zophar's word for Job: dissembled piety is double iniquity, the hottest place in hell its portion (Matt. 24:51), though the wicked may for a time be secure and merry.

themes: the triumph of the wicked is short

schools.summary: Gill: though his excellency mount to the heavens like the Assyrian's aspiration (Isa. 14:13) or Nebuchadnezzar's towering tree (Dan. 4:11), the loftier the rise the more complete the ruin.
Clarke reads the 'excellency' as Adam's original state in the image of God, cast down by sin; Wesley keeps it present — 'advanced to great dignity and authority.'
Henry supposes the prosperity as high as imagination reaches — not virtue but worldly wealth his excellency — bidding fair for universal monarchy, the pride and security but presages of ruin.

outliers.note: Reads the wicked man's 'excellency mounting to heaven' as an allusion to Adam's original state in God's image, ruined by the Fall — the chapter re-enacting Eden.

schools.summary: Gill spreads the ruin over both worlds — substance, body, and soul — the man perishing in his own corruption, loathsome as dung that is never returned to its place.
Clarke hears Zophar covertly deny the resurrection Job had just confessed: the wicked is dust returning to dust — 'a speech partaking of the malevolence of Zophar's spirit.'
Henry graduates the ruin: shameful (like his own dung, Isa. 66:24), surprising (desolate in a moment, Ps. 73:19), swift, utter, and final.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the run of verses in their rendering, the abrupt 'Where is he?' measuring the completeness of his disappearance.

outliers.note: Takes 'he shall perish for ever like his own dung' as Zophar hinting his disbelief in the resurrection Job asserted in the preceding chapter.

themes: a covert denial of the resurrection

schools.summary: Gill: 'fly away as a dream' — as a dream forgotten, or the illusion of a dream, like the hungry man who dreams he eats and wakes empty (Isa. 29:8).
Clarke: instead of rising with a new body as Job hoped (ch. 19:26), the man's flesh rots and his spirit is dissipated like a vapour, leaving only the bare impression that he existed.
Henry: a swift and utter destruction — chased away on the wings of his own terrors, gone like a dream, nothing left but matter to laugh at the folly of.

outliers.note: Reads the vanishing dream as Zophar's answer to Job's resurrection-hope of ch. 19:26 — no rising, only a spirit dissipated like vapour.

schools.summary: Gill weighs two senses — the eye no longer beholding his grandeur, or death having taken him quite away — preferring the latter from the parallel.
Henry: a final ruin — the eye that saw and adored him shall see him no more, his place giving him an eternal farewell, as Judas went to his own place (Acts 1:25).
Keil and Delitzsch keep the couplet's force, the personified 'place' sealing the man's absence.

themes: the doom of the man of the world's eye

schools.summary: Gill: the children, visited for the father's sins, seek to please the poor he oppressed, his hands restoring the plunder; but Jarchi turns the clause otherwise.
Clarke: the children reduced to serving the very poor (Gen. 9:25), the wealth restored; he records Good's 'his branches shall be involved in his iniquity' and Calmet's turn.
Henry: forced restitution — the clamour of the poor makes him send his children to beg pardon while his hands restore, not with a Zacchaeus's joy (Luke 19:8) but a vomit's pain.
Ellicott gives both poles: the children seek the poor's favour by making good what was taken, or 'the poor shall oppress his children.'

debates.question: What does the verse foretell of the wicked man's children?

sides.position: the sons appease the poor their father oppressed, restoring the plunder
the sons sunk into poverty and servitude
the poor turn at last upon the oppressor's children

schools.summary: Gill: youth's sins — pride, lust, luxury, intemperance — whose effects rot the flesh and the very bones; or, as some read, the man's 'secret sins' that God will find out.
Clarke leans (with Rosenmuller and Good) to 'his hidden things' — secret vices bringing his strength to the dust; Wesley: 'bones' the whole body, and 'the sin' the punishment of it.
Ellicott renders 'youthful vigour' (cf. Job 33:25; Ps. 89:46): though in the full vigour of life, it shall lie down with him in the dust.
Henry: the lusts of youth contract diseases that gnaw age (Prov. 5:11), the sins of youth lying down with him in the dust, iniquity upon his bones (Ezek. 32:27).

debates.question: What are the wicked man's bones 'full of'?

sides.position: the sins of his youth — moral sins and their bodily effects
youthful vigour, cut short and laid in the dust

themes: the sins that follow to the grave

schools.summary: Gill inclines to read the sweet 'wickedness' as covetousness, unlawful gain (Broughton, 'wrong'), though it bears sin in general, sweet to the unregenerate who drinks iniquity like water.
Clarke reads vv.12-16 as one sustained allegory — poison rolled under the tongue for its sweetness; Wesley pictures the epicure with his sweet morsel, kept and rolled to prolong the pleasure.
Ellicott: Zophar paints the wicked man as a gourmand or glutton — cruel and undiscerning if aimed at Job, perhaps charging him with an inordinate love of riches inferred from his wealth.

outliers.note: Judges the gourmand-portrait, if aimed at Job, a fresh instance of heartless cruelty and of Zophar's unfitness for the judge's office he assumes.

schools.summary: Gill: he spares the sin not by eating sparingly but by refusing to spit it out, sparing it as Saul spared Agag, a darling child of his heart.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he carefully cherished it and retained it in his palate,' setting the mouth's sweetness against the belly's bitterness, with the poets' golden-age rivers of milk.
Henry: keeping it in his mouth denotes obstinate persistence, or the fond re-acting of sin (Ezek. 23:19), or the hypocrite's concealment of a beloved lust.
Gill: the 'meat' is the sin the man lives on, a bread of deceit that turns in his bowels, the stomach revolting against it — the finishing of sin after the act.
Wesley: the meat turned from sweet to bitter, 'the gall of asps,' most bitter and pernicious, killing within a few hours without remedy.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'his bread is now changed in his bowels, it is the gall of vipers within him,' the turn falling in the belly.
Henry: the sweet sin becomes bitter in reflection, turned in the bowels like the book sweet in the mouth but bitter in the belly (Rev. 10:10), the fawning tongue proving the viper's.

themes: the meat turned in the bowels
conscience and the aftertaste of sin

schools.summary: Gill: the riches are another's, spoiled and devoured, reckoned as safe as meat in the belly, yet to be refunded whether he will or no.
Clarke keeps the medical realism: vomiting is the effect of poison, nature ejecting what would be its bane, so the ill-got wealth is cast out.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again; God shall cast them out of his belly' — his sickness and God's act at once.
Henry: either his uneasy conscience forces restitution with a vomit's reluctance, or God's providence casts the goods out while the love of the sin stays in the heart.

themes: God casts them from his belly
unjust gain will not stay down

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the asp's poison in head and teeth (Pliny), and on death by the asp as an ancient punishment of malefactors — sure and swift.
Clarke: the sweet, easily-besetting sin acts on the soul as the asp's poison on the body; the ancients held the venom to be the gall, exuded in the creature's rage.
Henry: what the man sucked so sweetly proves the poison of asps; when conscience wakes, the charming graces of sin turn into so many raging furies.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he sucked in the poison of vipers,' matching the earlier sweetness with the deadly draught that answers it.
Gill: the venom's thirst unslaked (like the rich man begging a drop, Luke 16:24), and the honey and butter a plenty of good things the man shall never taste.

Clarke: honey and butter, the yield of rich pasturage, a proverbial figure of the highest prosperity (Exod. 3:8; Isa. 7:22; Joel 3:18, and the classical poets); Wesley: he shall not 'see,' i.e. not enjoy, the satisfaction good men have.
Ellicott hears a possible clue to the book's age: the phrase may show not Zophar's reading of Moses but a common stock of proverbial speech, 'milk and honey' not original with the Pentateuch.
Henry: the man had promised himself rivers of sensual delight, and shall not see them, for the enjoyment sinks far below the raised expectation.

outliers.note: Weighs the 'honey and butter' phrase as bearing on the date of Job — a community of proverbial speech rather than dependence on the Pentateuch's 'land flowing with milk and honey.'

themes: milk and honey and the date of Job

schools.summary: Gill: 'that which he laboured for shall he restore' — the sweated gain wrung from him again, as the vomiting of the earlier verse had figured.

Keil and Delitzsch: because he gives out again what he acquired, he has no pleasure in it, the verse's lines keeping their independence; Ellicott allows the latter part probably right but offers 'according to the substance he hath gotten he shall not rejoice.'

Clarke ('O, how doctors disagree!') prefers 'he shall return to labour, but shall not eat,' with Good's dearth and Houbigant's and Coverdale's turns; Wesley: he shall not keep it, but part with his estate to make compensation for his wrongs.

debates.question: How is the difficult verse to be rendered?

sides.position: he must restore or give back what he laboured for, with no enjoyment of it
'he shall return to labour but not eat' / a dearth his recompense (Good, Coverdale)
'according to the substance he hath gotten he shall not rejoice'

schools.summary: Gill: a settled cruelty — he crushes the poor and leaves them so, without pity, and seizes 'a house which he builded not.'
Clarke: 'he hath broken in pieces the forsaken of the poor' — suffering the children left by the famished to perish, and throwing down a house he will not rebuild — aimed 'at Job all the while.'
Ellicott: for these insinuations there was not a vestige of ground, Job formally rebutting them in his apology of ch. 31.
Gill sets aside the gentler gloss (no contentment in his substance) for punishment: no quietness in belly or conscience, the restless craving now his sleepless plague.
Clarke: 'belly' stands for the whole inward man, the verse an endless, unfillable desire after secular good; Wesley: no peace in his mind, and he shall keep no part of his desirable things.
Henry: the ill-got wealth like undigested meat always upbraiding him — disquieted looking back by conscience and forward by care — none may enjoy comfortably what they got unjustly.

themes: the punishment fitted to the sin

schools.summary: Gill: 'none of his meat left' — none in the belly, none of his substance for himself or heirs; or none left to inherit, his family cut off.
Clarke gives Coverdale's 'he devoured so greedily he left nothing behind,' the man stripped of everything; Wesley: being known as totally ruined, no kindred will trouble for his relics.
Ellicott points the logic — 'there was nothing left that he devoured not, therefore his prosperity shall not endure.'
Henry: when he is dead no man shall look for his goods, nor any relation administer what he leaves.
Gill: amid a fulness of blessing he is reduced to straits — by fear of loss, a narrow spirit, dread of want, or sudden dispossession like Nebuchadnezzar.
Clarke calls it 'a fine saying,' true of every rich wicked man tormented by anxieties; Wesley reads the second clause of retribution in kind, punished by those as wicked as himself.

Ellicott renders 'the hand of every one that is in misery shall come upon him' — the wronged in retaliation; Keil and Delitzsch carry it into v.23, God sending His glowing wrath into his very flesh (cf. Zeph. 1:17).
Henry keeps the inward reading — in his fulness he is in straits through the anxieties of his own mind, like the rich fool of Luke 12:17.

debates.question: Whose 'hand' comes upon him in the midst of his sufficiency?

sides.position: the miserable and wronged, in retaliation
the wicked at large, or those as wicked as himself
the immediate hand of God's wrath

themes: straits in the fulness of sufficiency
the hand that comes upon him

schools.summary: Gill: 'about to fill his belly' both of an ordinary meal to satisfy nature and of gorging his barns, just as the wrath is poised to strike.

Henry: every word speaks terror — not justice only but the fury of God's wrath, rained like fire on Sodom (Ps. 11:6), no fence but Christ (Isa. 32:2), the tempest surprising him in his security (Luke 17:26).

Clarke hears an allusion to Israel's quails and the wrath rained while the flesh was in their mouths (Num. 11:33); Wesley: 'rain' names God the Author and the vehemence, and 'eating' is 'as it fell upon thy sons.'
Keil and Delitzsch confirm the grammar of the sudden sending-forth of wrath into his flesh.

outliers.note: Suspects Zophar's 'while he is eating' a cruel reflection on the death of Job's children, killed at their feast when the house fell (ch. 1:18) — Wesley hears the same barb, 'as it fell upon thy sons.'

schools.summary: Gill: fleeing the iron weapon (the flaming sword of justice) betrays a guilty conscience, yet none can outrun the hand of God.

Keil and Delitzsch set the clauses as a conditional pair — flee the iron and the brazen bow pierces him, the flight itself the punishment; Ellicott: 'if he escaped one mischance, another should overtake him.'
Clarke (with Coverdale): though he flee the iron weapon the steel bow strikes him through — all kinds of death await him.
Gill: the shaft drawn out, perhaps for healing but too late, the terrors upon him the terrors of an incurable death.

Keil and Delitzsch render the 'glittering sword' drawn from the gall, the bright steel from the seat of life; Ellicott: even escaping a second and third calamity, terrors still — 'true, yet utterly false in its application to Job.'
Clarke keeps the archery — the arrow drawn and passing through the body (Coverdale); Wesley: drawn from the gall, showing the wound deep and deadly, the terrors those of a death past cure.

outliers.note: Grants the death-agony 'all perfectly true in a sense, yea, even a truism, but utterly false in its application to Job himself.'

themes: the arrow drawn from the gall
true of the impenitent, false of Job

schools.summary: Gill: darkness laid up in his secret places — everlasting wrath among God's stores of vengeance, or judgment 'for his store' of secret sins brought to light.

Clarke: 'a fire not blown' a supernatural fire, lightning, with allusion to Korah's company (Num. 16:32); Wesley: miseries laid up by God, a fire kindled not by man but by God, the curse reaching his family.
Henry: a ruin that comes insensibly — a hidden darkness in his secret place, a fire not blown that consumes surely but slowly, as a worm withers the gourd.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'a fire that is not blown upon devoureth him,' feeding on what is left in his tent.

themes: the curse on what is left

schools.summary: Gill gives three senses of 'the heaven' — God who knows all secrets, the angels who gather out the wicked (Matt. 13:41), or the visible judgments descending from the sky.

Clarke: another allusion to Korah — the glory of the LORD revealing their iniquity, the earth swallowing them (Num. 16:31); Wesley: God a swift witness by extraordinary judgments, still reflecting on Job's fire from heaven, all creatures conspiring against him.
Henry: heaven reveals his iniquity and refuses to receive him, earth rises against him as the stomach against what is loathsome (Isa. 26:21) — whither can he go but to hell?
Ellicott: all nature combines for the ruin God has decreed — 'here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again; he has exhausted himself'; Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet plainly.

outliers.note: Marks the close of the dialogue: 'here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again; he has exhausted himself' — the third friend falls silent for good.

schools.summary: Gill: 'the increase of his house' — his children or his goods, or (Kimchi) the very walls of the dwelling, the stones pouring down in ruin.
Clarke: a further allusion to Korah, whose houses and goods perished (Num. 16:32); Wesley: the estate lost, flowing away like waters to return no more, in the day of God's wrath.
Henry: posterity rooted out and estate sunk together, the goods flowing away as fast as they came, the wrath he was treasuring up now paid out.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the produce of his house must vanish, flowing away in the day of God's wrath.'

themes: the increase of his house departs
wrath treasured up and paid out

schools.summary: Gill: the wicked man's 'portion,' though assigned from God, is at most worldly and confined to this life, hereafter an abode with the damned, banished from God's presence.

Clarke reads the quail-and-wrath allusions (Num. 11:33) as fixing the poem after that history, against the extreme antiquity claimed for Job; Wesley marks 'the heritage,' firm as an inheritance, set against what was got by fraud.

Henry: Zophar concludes like an orator with the settled portion of the wicked (Ezek. 33:8), yet 'therein Zophar was mistaken,' for the impenitent do not always meet such temporal ruin — the doctrine well explained and worst applied.
Keil and Delitzsch render the summary, 'this is the lot of the wicked man from Elohim, and the heritage decreed for him from God.'

debates.question: Does the wicked man's temporal ruin always fall as Zophar describes?

sides.position: the portion is settled and certain — the wicked shall surely die (Ezek. 33:8)
the impenitent do not always meet such temporal judgments — 'therein Zophar was mistaken'

outliers.note: Turns the closing verse into a digression on the date of Job, reading the quail, manna, and Korah allusions (with the bishop of Killala) as proof the poem was written after the Pentateuch's history.

themes: the portion of the wicked from God
the date of the book of Job
